interactive.title: Slide the digits
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens on a place-value strip. Each column is one place, headed by what a digit there is worth, from millions on the left to ten-millionths on the right, and the decimal point is fixed between the units and the tenths. Under the strip the same number is written as a front number times a power of ten. On the first screen a stepper sets the power, n, from −6 to 6, opening at 0 with 4.7 on the strip. Each step up multiplies by 10, and multiplying by 10 makes every digit worth ten times as much, which is what the place on its left is worth, so every digit slides one place left and the point stays put. Three steps up give 4.7 × 10³ = 4700, with zeros holding the empty places. Screen 3 steps down: each step divides by 10, as in lesson 2, so the digits slide right, and 4.7 × 10⁻³ = 0.0047. Screen 5 holds the number at 0.0047 and slides only the front number: 47 × 10⁻⁴, 4.7 × 10⁻³ and 0.47 × 10⁻² are all 0.0047, because a front number 10 times bigger goes with a power one smaller. A Standard form switch snaps it to one figure before the point, 4.7 × 10⁻³. Screen 7 adds an Engineering notation switch, which snaps the power to a multiple of 3, with 1 up to, but not including, 1000 in front, and shows the prefix for that power, with a teal box on its place. Its stepper runs n from −6 to 3 in amps, opening at 0 on 4.7 A. Stepping down gives 470 mA, 47 mA and 4.7 mA, then 470 µA, 47 µA and 4.7 µA, and stepping up gives 47 A, 470 A and 4.7 kA, so the digits slide every step and the prefix changes only at every third step. 10⁰ has no prefix. A small table lists the prefixes: G 10⁹, M 10⁶, k 10³, m 10⁻³, µ 10⁻⁶, n 10⁻⁹ and p 10⁻¹², with centi, 10⁻², set apart as a prefix that is not a multiple of 3. Screen 9 multiplies with prefixes, using Ohm's law, V = I × R: 2 mA through 5 kΩ is 2 × 10⁻³ × 5 × 10³, the front numbers multiply to 10 and the powers add to 0, so 10 × 10⁰ = 10 V. Screen 11 adds: 4 × 10³ + 5 × 10², the first slid to 40 × 10², so the powers match, then 45 × 10² = 4.5 × 10³. Screen 11 also shows the slip of adding the powers: 9 × 10⁵ would be 900,000, far from 4500. Screens 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and 11 show an idea, and screens 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 ask you to try it: 3.2 × 10⁴ written out, the power for 0.0047 A, 470 × 10⁻⁵ in standard form, 0.000047 F with a prefix, and 4 mA through 2.2 kΩ. Screens 12 and 13 mix them: two loads of 3 × 10⁴ W and 2 × 10³ W added, and 9 V across 1.5 MΩ, where dividing takes the powers away, 10⁰ ÷ 10⁶ = 10⁻⁶, giving 6 µA. A puzzle offers three answers, and a wrong pick draws its slip as a red row on the strip under the question's own rows, so you can see where its digits land.
interactive.ignores: The strip runs from millions to ten-millionths only; bigger and smaller numbers need more places and work the same way. The digits slide and the point stays fixed; moving the point the other way gives the same answer. Every number is exact here, while a measured value carries only the figures that were measured: 4700 written out does not show whether its zeros were measured, and 4.7 × 10³ shows two figures. Only the prefixes in the table are drawn; others exist, such as deci and hecto, and like centi they are not multiples of 3. The currents, resistances and voltages are examples.

explain.text:
Multiplying by a power of ten slides the digits past a fixed decimal point, one place for each 10, and each power of ten you are likely to meet that is a multiple of 3, other than 0, has a short name in front of the unit, so 0.0047 A is 4.7 × 10⁻³ A, or 4.7 mA. Start from place value. In 4.7 the 4 stands for four units and the 7 for seven tenths. Multiply by 10 and each digit is worth ten times as much, which is exactly what the place on its left is worth, so every digit slides one place left and the decimal point stays where it is. 10³ is three 10s multiplied, as in lesson 1, so 4.7 × 10³ slides the digits three places left, to 4700, and zeros hold the empty places. A negative power gives one over the number,[^5] so 10⁻³ is one over 1000, a thousandth, and 4.7 × 10⁻³ slides the digits three places right, to 0.0047.

Because the digits can slide either way, one number can be written many ways: 0.0047 is 47 × 10⁻⁴, 4.7 × 10⁻³ and 0.47 × 10⁻². Make the front number 10 times bigger and the power must drop by one to keep the same number, so a bigger front number goes with a smaller power. Move the power the same way as the front number and the number changes: 470 × 10⁻⁵ is 0.0047, but 4.7 × 10⁻⁷ is 0.00000047, ten thousand times smaller. [[Standard form]] settles on one of these: a number between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of ten, also called standard index form or scientific notation.[^6] Written as A × 10ⁿ, with A the front number, Bitesize pins the range down as 1 ≤ A < 10: 1 is allowed and 10 is not.[^7] So 0.0047 is 4.7 × 10⁻³, and 47 × 10⁻⁴, with two figures before the point, is the same number but not standard form.

In electrical work the power is usually kept to a multiple of 3. Each step of 3 is one comma group of three digits, the groups you already write in 32,000 and 4,700,000, and each of those powers you are likely to meet, other than 0, has a [[prefix]], a letter in front of the unit that stands for that power of ten. Milli, m, is a thousandth, 10⁻³,[^1] so 4.7 × 10⁻³ A is 4.7 mA. The BIPM's list of SI prefixes gives kilo, k, as 10³, mega, M, as 10⁶, micro, µ, as 10⁻⁶ and further out giga, G, as 10⁹,[^2] and Fiore's lab manual adds nano, n, 10⁻⁹, and pico, p, 10⁻¹².[^3] In [[engineering notation]] the power is always a multiple of 3, the only difference from scientific notation,[^8] and a prefix stands in for that power.[^3] Taking the multiple of 3 at or below the number's own power leaves a front number from 1 up to, but not including, 1000, so 1000 mA is written 1 A. NIST's guide to the SI reports a common recommendation: use only the prefixes for powers of ten that are multiples of 3, chosen so the number in front is between 0.1 and 1000.[^4] That range starts lower, so 0.47 mA meets it, while engineering notation writes the same current as 470 µA; neither is wrong. So the prefix changes only at every third place: 4.7 mA, 47 mA, 470 mA, then 4.7 A. Centi, c, as in cm, is 10⁻²:[^2] a prefix, but not one engineering notation uses. A prefix is a power of ten, so lesson 1's laws work on it. Multiplying adds the powers:[^9] 2 mA × 5 kΩ is 2 × 10⁻³ × 5 × 10³ = 10 × 10⁰, and any base to the power of zero equals 1,[^10] so that is 10 V. Dividing takes the powers away: 9 V ÷ 1.5 kΩ is 9 ÷ 1.5 = 6 with 10⁰ ÷ 10³ = 10⁻³, so 6 × 10⁻³ A = 6 mA. Adding is different, because only the front numbers add, and only when the powers match: 3 × 10⁴ + 2 × 10³ = 30 × 10³ + 2 × 10³ = 32 × 10³ = 3.2 × 10⁴, which is 30,000 + 2,000 = 32,000. Adding the powers instead gives 5 × 10⁷, which is 50,000,000.

**Multiplying by 10ⁿ slides the digits n places, left for a positive n and right for a negative one, and each power you are likely to meet that is a multiple of 3, other than 0, has a prefix, so 0.0047 A = 4.7 × 10⁻³ A = 4.7 mA.[^1]**

analogy.text: On a price or a pay offer you may have seen £4,700 written as £4.7k. That is the same move: the k stands for 1000, so the digits slide three places and the k carries the difference, just as 4,700 Ω is 4.7 kΩ.
analogy.breaks: In money, m often means a million, as in £2m. In units, small m is milli, a thousandth, and capital M is mega, a million, so 2 mΩ is two thousandths of an ohm and 2 MΩ is two million ohms. Units are strict about capitals where everyday writing is not.

practice.text:
To write a number in standard form:
- Slide the digits until one figure other than zero sits before the point: 0.00047 becomes 4.7.
- Count the places you slid. That count is the size of the power.
- Make the power negative if the number is less than 1, and positive if it is 10 or more: 0.00047 = 4.7 × 10⁻⁴.

To give it a prefix:
- Move the power down to the nearest multiple of 3, sliding the digits to match: 4.7 × 10⁻⁴ = 470 × 10⁻⁶.
- Swap the power for its prefix: 470 × 10⁻⁶ A = 470 µA. A power of 0 needs no prefix.
- Check by sliding back: a bigger front number must go with a smaller power.

**Rule of thumb:** A number of 10 or more has a positive power, a number below 1 a negative power, and a number from 1 up to 10 has 10⁰. Kilo and milli cancel, 10³ × 10⁻³ = 10⁰ = 1, so milliamps times kilohms gives volts. Kilo times micro is milli, 10³ × 10⁻⁶ = 10⁻³.

**On a calculator:** enter a number in standard form with the ×10ˣ key (EXP or EE on some calculators), which keeps the whole number together, so no brackets are needed.[^11] 9 ÷ 1.5 ×10ˣ 3 gives 0.006. Typed as 9 ÷ 1.5 × 10 ^ 3, the calculator works out 9 ÷ 1.5 first and then multiplies by 1000, giving 6000 (worked out by the order of operations, not from this lesson's sources). With ordinary keys, put brackets round the whole number: 9 ÷ (1.5 × 10 ^ 3).

**Worked example:** Say a relay coil of 4.7 kΩ carries 2.5 mA. The voltage across it is V = I × R = 2.5 × 10⁻³ A × 4.7 × 10³ Ω. Multiply the front numbers, 2.5 × 4.7 = 11.75, and add the powers, −3 + 3 = 0, so V = 11.75 × 10⁰ V = 11.75 V. And a 330 µF capacitor? 330 × 10⁻⁶ F = 3.3 × 10⁻⁴ F = 0.00033 F.

**Common mistakes**
- Two figures before the point: 47 × 10⁻⁴ is the right number but not standard form; it is 4.7 × 10⁻³.
- Moving the power the same way as the front number: 470 × 10⁻⁵ is 4.7 × 10⁻³, not 4.7 × 10⁻⁷. A smaller front number needs a bigger power.
- Counting zeros instead of places: 0.0047 has two zeros after the point but is 4.7 × 10⁻³.
- Adding the powers in a sum: 3 × 10⁴ + 2 × 10³ is 3.2 × 10⁴, not 5 × 10⁷.
- Mixing up m and M: 1 mΩ is a thousandth of an ohm, 1 MΩ a million ohms. And kilo is a small k: kV, not KV.

A place-value strip: each column is headed by what a digit there is worth, and the decimal point is fixed. The currents, resistances, loads and capacitor are examples.

Prefixes, one for every third power

G, M, k, m, µ and c from the BIPM's list of SI prefixes; n and p from Fiore's lab manual.

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the digits of 4.7 sliding three places right past a fixed point to 0.0047, which is 4.7 × 10⁻³ A or 4.7 mA, when you step the power down to −3.

checks.label: So a negative power gives the reciprocal of the number, 1 over the number: on the first screen, at every power from −1 to −6, the strip reads 4.7 times 1 over that many 10s, and its line "10ⁿ = 1 ÷ …" adds up

In standard form, numbers are recorded as a number between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of ten: the Standard form view of the current at every power from −6 to 3, the front-number screen at 4.7 × 10⁻³, and the right answer to 470 × 10⁻⁵ each leave a front number from 1 up to 10 whose digits, slid by its power, are the number on the strip

Prefix symbols should be chosen so that numerical values are between 0.1 and 1000, and only prefixes for 10 raised to a multiple of 3 should be used: in Engineering notation, at every power from −6 to 3, the front number is from 1 up to 1000, its power is a multiple of 3 with that prefix (none at 10⁰), and front number × that power is the current on the strip
Milli (symbol m) is a unit prefix denoting a factor of one thousandth (10⁻³): in Engineering notation at power −3 the current 0.0047 A reads 4.7 mA, and the line 1 mA = 10⁻³ A = 0.001 A adds up

The base numbers are the same, so add the indices together (9³ × 9⁵ = 9⁸): 2 mA × 5 kΩ slides 3 places right for the m and 3 back for the k, landing on 10 × 10⁰ V = 10 V, and 4 mA × 2.2 kΩ lands on 8.8 V
Any base to the power of zero equals 1: the first screen at power 0 shows 10⁰ = 1 and leaves 4.7 unslid, and 10 × 10⁰ V and 8.8 × 10⁰ V sit exactly where 10 and 8.8 sit

giga G 10⁹, mega M 10⁶, kilo k 10³, centi c 10⁻², milli m 10⁻³, micro µ 10⁻⁶: the prefix table, the strip's tags and the reading of a prefixed unit give each of these its power, and the note gives centi 10⁻²
For engineering notation the exponent is always a multiple of three, and E−9 = nano (n), E−12 = pico (p): every power in the prefix table is a multiple of 3, with n at 10⁻⁹ and p at 10⁻¹²

Each step up slides every digit exactly one place left: on the first screen the number at each power is 10 times the one at the power below, and the zeros only fill places between the digits and the point
Every row drawn on every screen, in every state, reads back its own number from its digits, and every line of working adds up
The prefix changes only at every third place: in Engineering notation from 10³ down to 10⁻⁶ the prefix runs k, then none three times, m three times, µ three times
Each puzzle accepts only its right answer; the right answer's row lands on the number asked for; each wrong pick draws one row of its own in red, holding the number it names
Every demonstration has arrived within 5 s of its screen opening, nothing before the 0.35 s screen fade; every answer's motion, and every move on a live screen, within 3 s

applied.problem: NIST does not itself recommend this: its guide says 'It is often recommended that' prefixes be chosen so values are 0.1 to 1000 and powers are multiples of 3. Also, SI prefixes stop at 10^30 and 10^-30, so 'each multiple of 3 has a prefix' needs narrowing.
